items.title: Mozambique attracts US$1.88 billion in FDI in H1
items.summary: The total comprised inflows of US$1.286 billion (€1.091 billion) in the first quarter of 2026 and US$594.5 million (€517 million) in the second quarter, according to statistical data from the Bank of Mozambique Despite the slowdown observed between April and June, the structure of foreign investment remains largely dominated by megaprojects associated with natural resources, particularly natural gas, oil and mining, which continue to absorb most of the external capital directed towards the Mozambican economy In the documents accompanying the Economic and Social Plan and State Budget (PESOE), the Government projected a new historic high of US$5.88 billion (€4.988 billion) in FDI for 2026, driven mainly by progress on liquefied natural gas projects in the north of the country In the first quarter, the extractive industries attracted US$1.209 billion (€1.048 billion), equivalent to approximately 94% of all FDI received by the country during that period, highlighting the decisive weight of major energy and mining projects in attracting foreign investment The dominance of this sector…

items.title: Mozambique: Moderate flood risk in Maputo River basin after South Africa’s Pongolapoort Dam increases discharge rate
items.summary: The National Directorate for Water Resources Management (DNGRH) yesterday warned of a moderate risk of flooding in the Maputo River basin after Pongolapoort Dam, also known as Jozini Dam, in northern KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, opened its sluice gates on Saturday, 8 November, raising the discharge rate to 700 cubic metres per second The directorate said the effects could be felt in Mozambique within 48 hours of the announcement, with the Maputo River expected to continue rising and potentially reach its peak during that period. The increased flow could worsen flooding on riverside farmland and disrupt road traffic in Catuane, Salamanga and Tinonganine, in Matutuíne district, Maputo province, southern Mozambique The DNGRH advised riverside communities to avoid crossing the river or entering flooded areas, particularly farmland.

items.title: Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains
items.summary: Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy.

items.title: Government to conduct inspections in over 5,000 schools
items.summary: Maputo, 11 Nov (AIM) – The Mozambican education ministry plans to carry out inspections in 5,250 schools in 2027 “as part of efforts to strengthen oversight and improve the quality of education.” According to Edson Macuácua, education minister, speaking at the opening of the First National Training Seminar for Inspectors, held in Ponta do Ouro, southern Maputo province, the target represents 35 per cent of the country’s educational establishments, up from 4,880 schools (32.5 per cent) targeted in 2026. However, the country’s education system demands concrete measures more that just inspections. The country’s National Association of Teachers (ANAPRO) has been calling for a response to the long-running dispute over the government’s failure to pay teachers for overtime since 2023. ANAPRO once said that it has lost confidence in the government institutions it was negotiating with. Anapro claims that all means of dialogue had been tried, without any satisfactory reply to their demands.

items.title: Gaza needs 18 million meticais to tackle drought
items.summary: Maputo, 11 Nov (AIM) – Mozambique’s relief agency, the National Disaster Management Institute (INGD), needs over 18 million meticais (just over 280,000 US dollars at the current exchange rate) to respond to the drought caused by the El Niño phenomenon in southern province of Gaza, which is expected to affect 422,000 households. According to INGD in Gaza, these figures serve as a guide for planning and mobilizing resources to assist vulnerable communities. The 2026/27 rainy season points to normal rainfall in the Northern provinces of Nampula, Cabo Delgado, and Niassa. However, it points out a risk of severe drought in 76 districts across the southern provinces of Maputo, Gaza, Inhambane, and central provinces of Sofala, Manica, and Tete, due to the influence of the El Niño phenomenon.

items.title: Spain: Housing crisis prompts general strike
items.summary: Workers across nearly all industries have taken to the picket lines as rents soar and the housing crunch worsens. The crisis is the main political debate ahead of Spain's November 29 elections Workers across Spain gathered en mass on Wednesday, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country This is the first general strike in Spain in 14 years, amid a worsening cost of living and lack of housing crisis that has left many unable to support themselves Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29 The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties.

items.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
items.summary: Agnes Shikoli says she fears either drowning, or being crushed by her house "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives "Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls.
